---
title: "The conversion is a quality process"
---

The stages before this one treat the study's documents as input. This chapter is about what
happens to those documents on the way through — which turned out to be the most useful thing
the exercise produced, and the part that transfers to any study.

## What this is

A person reading a protocol can pass over an ambiguity without noticing. They fill the gap from
experience, and often fill it correctly. A generator cannot. Asked to produce a structured
estimand, it must be told the population; asked to bind a derivation, it must be told which
record is the baseline. There is no option to proceed on the assumption that everybody knows.

**That is why the conversion finds things: not because the tool is clever, but because it cannot
skip.** Structuring a document is a reading of unusual severity, and the questions it raises
were available to anyone reading carefully — they were simply never forced.

The kinds of thing that surface are consistent across studies:

- **The same fact, stated differently in two documents.** A synopsis and a body section that
  disagree on a ratio or a population, where neither is obviously the authority.
- **Something the analysis needs that no document defines.** A variable the analysis plan names
  that no specification produces, or a flag nothing derives.
- **A convention assumed but never written.** Which record is the baseline is the example this
  whole book turns on: universally understood, rarely stated, and resolvable two ways.
- **A change made in place.** A document amended without a version, so two readers holding
  what they believe is the same document hold different text.

None of these is a mistake in the ordinary sense. They are decisions that were never recorded as
decisions, and they survive because prose tolerates them.

## What you do

The loop has four steps, and the third is the one people skip.

1. **Record the question when it arises**, rather than resolving it silently. The temptation at
   stage 1 or stage 3 is to pick the sensible reading and carry on, because you are trying to
   get an endpoint authored. Write it down instead.
2. **Decide where the fix belongs.** Almost always the source, not your copy.
3. **Take it to whoever owns the document**, as a draft they can read — not as a defect report
   and not as a patch already applied. What you have is a question that structuring the
   document raised; they have the context to answer it.
4. **When the source changes, re-run everything against it.** A loop that stops before this is
   an opinion, not a correction.

In this project that meant two issues raised on the study's own repository —
[#27](https://github.com/OpenTrialReporting/torivumab-nsclc-301/issues/27) and
[#53](https://github.com/OpenTrialReporting/torivumab-nsclc-301/issues/53) — each shown as a
draft before it was filed, and each closed by the study's owner. The register of what was raised
lives with the study, where it belongs, and not in this book.

## What you should see

Numbers that move.

When the source was corrected and the analysis re-run, every figure in this book changed.
That is uncomfortable and it is the point: if correcting the documents had left the results
identical, the corrections would have been cosmetic. The chain is only worth building if it is
connected at both ends, and a moving number is the evidence that it is.

## What to look out for

**Fix the source, not your copy.** Patching your own derived version is faster, and it is the
decision that quietly ends the loop: from then on your copy and the source disagree, the
disagreement grows with every correction, and nobody downstream of the source ever benefits.
This project went the other way, and the cost was re-pinning and re-running twice in one day.

**They are questions, not findings.** The framing decides whether you get an answer. *"Which
record is baseline — the plan is consistent with two readings"* is a question the author can
answer. *"The plan is ambiguous"* is a verdict on their work, and invites a defence rather than
a decision.

**Draft, show, wait.** Nothing here was filed without the owner seeing it first and saying yes.
That is slower than filing directly and it is the difference between a collaboration and an
audit.

**Beware the easy version of this argument.** In this project the person who found the questions
and the person who owned the study were the same person, which made the loop fast and
frictionless. Across an organisation it is neither. The mechanism is real; the speed here is
not representative, and anyone planning on it should assume the conversation is the slow part.
